summary: For 12–14 year olds: establish the atmosphere's composition (~78% nitrogen, ~21% oxygen, ~1% argon, ~0.04% CO2), show that CO2 is a trace gas with an outsized climatic effect, explain the greenhouse mechanism (sunlight in, outgoing infrared absorbed and re-radiated), distinguish the natural (habitable) from the enhanced (warming) greenhouse effect, and connect human fossil-fuel burning and deforestation to rising CO2, rising global temperature, and at least one specific consequence (e.g. rising sea levels, more extreme weather), using evidence (the Keeling CO2 curve and the century-scale temperature record). Keep it qualitative and mechanism-based at KS3; avoid radiative-forcing maths. Several complementary media are offered: a driveable model, a diagram/cross-section scaffold, an evidence-focused dialogue, and a checkpoint, each with a stated affordance and limit.
misconceptions: Thinking CO2 makes up a large fraction of the air, rather than only ~0.04%.
Confusing the greenhouse effect with the ozone hole, or believing warming comes from a 'hole' letting more sunlight in.
Believing the natural greenhouse effect is bad, missing that it keeps Earth habitable and only the enhanced effect is the problem.
Thinking CO2 blocks incoming sunlight rather than trapping outgoing infrared.
Assuming because CO2 is a tiny percentage it cannot matter for climate.

activities.title: Drive a two-part climate model: greenhouse effect and emissions
steps: Start from the greenhouse view: watch sunlight stream onto the surface and infrared radiate back out toward space.

Move a CO2 control to thicken the atmospheric 'blanket' so more outgoing infrared is re-radiated back down, and read the thermometer as it changes; compare the natural baseline level with an enhanced (higher-CO2) level.
Read a composition pie showing CO2 as roughly 0.04% of the air, then state in your own words how such a small slice can still change the temperature you just observed.
Switch to the emissions view and raise the fossil-fuel-burning and deforestation controls; watch the atmospheric-CO2 graph rise (echoing the real Keeling curve) and a global-temperature trace follow.
Write the causal chain the model produced: burn fossil fuels / deforest → CO2 rises → more infrared trapped → global temperature rises.
activities.insight: CO2 is a trace gas (~0.04%) yet climatically powerful because it absorbs and re-emits outgoing infrared; human emissions raise CO2, which raises global temperature — a cause-and-effect chain the learner generates rather than a slogan.

activities.title: Explore a labelled atmosphere cross-section and greenhouse diagram
steps: Examine a layered illustration of the atmosphere with a composition pie (78% N2, 21% O2, ~1% Ar, ~0.04% CO2) and name the main gases in order.
Tap the Sun, the surface, and CO2 molecules on a greenhouse-effect diagram to reveal how incoming sunlight is absorbed and outgoing infrared is trapped and re-radiated.
Identify human sources of CO2 (fossil-fuel burning, deforestation) highlighted on the diagram.
activities.insight: Orient to atmospheric composition and the in/out radiation idea: nitrogen dominates, CO2 is a trace gas, and the greenhouse mechanism acts on outgoing infrared.

activities.title: Question a climate scientist about the evidence
steps: Ask an in-role climate scientist 'how do we know?' questions about rising CO2 and temperature.
Have the scientist explain the Keeling CO2 curve and the century-scale temperature record and where the data come from.
Ask the scientist about one specific consequence of the warming (e.g. rising sea levels or more extreme weather) and how it follows from higher global temperatures.
Answer the scientist's probing questions, e.g. why a 0.04% gas can matter and how the greenhouse effect differs from the ozone hole.
activities.insight: The human–CO2–warming link rests on readable evidence (rising CO2 curve, temperature record) and leads to concrete consequences such as rising sea levels or more extreme weather; 'how do we know?' reasoning distinguishes mechanism from slogan.

activities.title: Checkpoint: composition, mechanism, causal chain, consequence and graph reading
steps: Set or select the approximate percentages of N2, O2, Ar and CO2 (e.g. 78% / 21% / ~1% / ~0.04%).
Choose which gases are greenhouse gases and which are not.
Put the causal chain in order: burn fossil fuels → CO2 rises → more infrared trapped → temperature rises.
Identify one specific consequence of climate change (e.g. rising sea levels, more extreme weather).
Read a CO2/temperature graph and state what the trend shows and why it matters.
activities.insight: Consolidate the facts and the chain: correct composition, which gases trap infrared, the ordered cause-and-effect, a named consequence, and interpretation of trend data.

checkQuestion: A student says 'the air is mostly oxygen, and carbon dioxide makes up a big chunk of it too — that's why more CO₂ is warming the planet so much.' What's actually the biggest gas in the air, and roughly how much of it is CO₂? Then the important part: if CO₂ is such a tiny fraction, explain how adding more of it can still change the climate.
checkAnswer: Air is mostly NITROGEN (~78%), then oxygen (~21%); CO₂ is only a tiny fraction (~0.04%). Even so, CO₂ is a greenhouse gas: it absorbs and re-emits the infrared (heat) radiation the Earth gives off, trapping energy in the atmosphere. A small percentage change in a powerful heat-trapping gas has a large warming effect. Full marks correct the composition AND explain warming by the greenhouse (infrared-trapping) mechanism, not by CO₂'s abundance.
